The question could apply to Next.js or Angular. The context covers both, but only Next.js has anything on meta descriptions.

## Next.js (App Router)

Export a `metadata` object (or a `generateMetadata` function) from each page or layout file. [5] Each page's export sets that page's title:

```tsx
import type { Metadata } from 'next'

export const metadata: Metadata = {
  title: 'My Page Title',
}

export default function Page() {
  return '...'
}
```
[4]

The docs list `title` and `description` as examples of metadata you can define this way [5]. The provided context doesn't show the exact `description` field syntax or how to use `generateMetadata` for dynamic values. See the [metadata options reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-metadata) for details [4].

If you're migrating from the `pages` directory, this export replaces `next/head` [4].

## Angular

Angular sets titles per route with the `title` property, and updates the page title automatically when the route activates [3]:

```ts
const routes: Routes = [
  { path: '', component: Home, title: 'Home Page' },
  { path: 'about', component: About, title: 'About Us' },
];
```
[3]

For dynamic titles, use a `ResolveFn`, or extend the `TitleStrategy` class for a custom approach [3].

questions.answer:
The question doesn't name a framework, so here is what the docs provided say for each one.

## Next.js
Use the `next/image` component. Its improved behavior (less client-side JavaScript, easier styling, better accessibility, native browser lazy loading) is the default as of version 13 [2]. You can tune optimization in `next.config.js`:

- **`qualities`**: an allowlist of quality values. It is required starting with Next.js 16. If the `quality` prop doesn't match an entry, the closest allowed value is used [4].
- **`formats`**: the output formats. Next.js reads the request's `Accept` header to pick the best one, and the first match in the array wins [4].

```js
module.exports = {
  images: {
    qualities: [25, 50, 75, 100],
  },
}
```
[4]

## Angular
Use the built-in `NgOptimizedImage` directive, which generates `srcset`s automatically [3]. Other ways to fix oversized images are to use a smaller source image or add a `srcset` by hand for different layouts [3].

## React Native
Place static images in your source tree and reference them with `require`. Add `@2x` and `@3x` variants so the bundler serves the one matching the device's screen density [1].

```tsx
<Image source={require('./img/check.png')} />
```
[1]

Only images that are actually used get packaged into the app, and the image name in `require` must be known statically [1].

## Not covered

questions.answer:
Prefix the variable name with `NEXT_PUBLIC_`. By default, environment variables are only available on the server, and the prefix is what exposes one to the browser [1].

```txt filename=".env"
NEXT_PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ID=abcdefghijk
```

At build time, Next.js inlines the value into the JavaScript bundle sent to the client, replacing references to `process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ID` with the hard-coded value from the environment where you ran `next build` [5].

```js filename="pages/index.js"
import setupAnalyticsService from '../lib/my-analytics-service'

// 'NEXT_PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ID' can be used here as it's prefixed by 'NEXT_PUBLIC_'.
// It will be transformed at build time to `setupAnalyticsService('abcdefghijk')`.
setupAnalyticsService(process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ID)
```
[5]

**Caveats:**
- After the build, the app no longer responds to changes to these variables. For example, with a single Docker image deployed to multiple environments, all `NEXT_PUBLIC_` values stay frozen at their build-time values [5].
- If you need runtime values in the browser, you have to set up your own API to provide them to the client, either on demand or during initialization [5].
- Dynamic lookups are not inlined [5]. The provided context cuts off before showing the example, so it doesn't give further detail.

questions.answer:
## Setting up Jest in Next.js

Next.js has had built-in Jest configuration since Next.js 12. [3]

### 1. Install dev dependencies

```bash
npm install -D jest jest-environment-jsdom @testing-library/react @testing-library/dom @testing-library/jest-dom ts-node @types/jest
```

The docs also give equivalent commands for pnpm, yarn and bun. [3]

### 2. Generate a Jest config

```bash
npm init jest@latest
```

This walks you through a series of prompts and creates a `jest.config.ts` or `jest.config.js` file. [3]

### 3. Use `next/jest` in the config

Update the config file to use `next/jest`, which is a transformer with all the configuration Jest needs to work with Next.js. [3]

The docs provided don't include the example config code for this step, so I can't show it here.

### 4. (Optional) Handle module path aliases

If your project uses module path aliases, match the `paths` option in `tsconfig.json`/`jsconfig.json` with `moduleNameMapper` in `jest.config.js`: [2]

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "baseUrl": "./",
    "paths": {
      "@/components/*": ["components/*"]
    }
  }
}
```

```js
moduleNameMapper: {
  // ...
  '^@/components/(.*)$': '<rootDir>/components/$1',
}
```

### Limitations

Jest doesn't currently support `async` Server Components. You can unit test synchronous Server and Client Components, but the docs recommend E2E tests for `async` components. [4]

### Further reading

There's a [Next.js with Jest example](https://github.com/vercel/next.js/tree/canary/examples/with-jest) in the Next.js repo. [5]

The docs provided don't cover the remaining steps, such as adding a test script or writing your first test.

questions.answer:
Yes, if you configure Jest with `next/jest`. It loads `.env` (and all variants) into `process.env` [1][2]. For this to work, pass your app's path via the `dir` option so `next/jest` can load `next.config.js` and `.env` files [1]:

```ts
import nextJest from 'next/jest.js'

const createJestConfig = nextJest({
  dir: './',
})
```

A few details about which files are used in the `test` environment:

- Test defaults load when `NODE_ENV` is `test`, which testing tools usually set for you. You can put test-specific values in a `.env.test` file [3].
- `.env.development` and `.env.production` are not loaded in the test environment [3].
- `.env.local` is not loaded, so tests produce the same results for everyone [3].

If you want to test environment variables directly, load them manually in a separate setup script or in your `jest.config.ts` [1]. You can use `loadEnvConfig` from `@next/env`, for example in a Jest global setup file [3]:

```js
import { loadEnvConfig } from '@next/env'

export default async () => {
  const projectDir = process.cwd()
  loadEnvConfig(projectDir)
}
```

questions.question: What's the difference between toBe and toEqual?
questions.searchedQuestion: What's the difference between toBe and toEqual?

retrieved.headingPath: Expect > Matchers > .toEqual(value)
Using Matchers > Numbers
Expect > Expect > expect(value)
Using Matchers > Common Matchers

questions.answer:
**`.toBe`** checks exact equality using `Object.is`. [4] Use it for primitives or when you need the very same reference.

**`.toEqual`** recursively compares all properties of objects and arrays ("deep" equality). It also uses `Object.is` for primitive values. [1][4] Use it to check the contents of an object or array. [4]

In the docs' example, two separate objects with the same properties pass `toEqual` but fail `toBe`, because they are not the exact same object:

```js
const can1 = { flavor: 'grapefruit', ounces: 12 };
const can2 = { flavor: 'grapefruit', ounces: 12 };

expect(can1).toEqual(can2);   // passes
expect(can1).not.toBe(can2);  // passes
```
[1]

**Other notes:**
- For numbers, `toBe` and `toEqual` are equivalent. [2]
- `toEqual` ignores object keys with `undefined` properties, `undefined` array items, array sparseness, and object type mismatch. Use `.toStrictEqual` if you need those to count. [1][4]
- For errors, `toEqual` only considers the `message` property. The docs recommend `.toThrow` for testing errors. [1]
- For floating point numbers, use `toBeCloseTo` rather than `toEqual`, to avoid rounding errors. [2]

questions.answer:
Run Jest with the `--updateSnapshot` flag to re-generate the snapshot artifacts:

```bash
jest --updateSnapshot
```

You can use the single-character `-u` instead. This re-generates snapshots for all failing snapshot tests. [2]

**Before you update:**
- If any failing tests are caused by an unintentional bug, fix the bug first. Otherwise you'll record snapshots of the buggy behavior. [2]

**Limit which snapshots are updated:**
- Pass `--testNamePattern` along with the update flag to re-record only the tests that match the pattern. [2]

**Interactive alternative:**
- In watch mode, you can update failed snapshots interactively. Jest steps through the failed snapshots one test at a time, lets you review the output, and lets you either update each snapshot or skip to the next. Afterward, it gives you a summary and returns to watch mode. [3]

**CI note:**
- With `--ci`, Jest doesn't automatically store new snapshots. Instead, it fails the test and requires you to run Jest with `--updateSnapshot`. [5]

questions.answer:
Use the `BackHandler` API, which detects hardware back button presses on Android and lets you register listeners and control how your app responds. It is Android-only. [5]

How subscriptions behave:

- Subscriptions are called in reverse order, so the last registered one runs first. [5]
- If a subscription returns `true`, earlier-registered subscriptions are not called. [5]
- If no subscription returns `true`, or none are registered, the default back behavior runs and exits the app. [5]
- If your app shows an open `Modal`, `BackHandler` publishes no events. See the `Modal` docs on `onRequestClose`. [5]

**With React Navigation:** follow their guide on [Custom Android back button behaviour](https://reactnavigation.org/docs/custom-android-back-button-handling/). [2]

**With an Android Fragment integration (native host Activity):** the host Activity isn't a `ReactActivity`, so it must implement `DefaultHardwareBackBtnHandler`. [1]

```kotlin
import com.facebook.react.modules.core.DefaultHardwareBackBtnHandler

class MainActivity : AppCompatActivity(), DefaultHardwareBackBtnHandler {

    // ...

    override fun invokeDefaultOnBackPressed() {
        onBackPressedDispatcher.onBackPressed()
    }
}
```
[1]

`Activity.onBackPressed()` has been deprecated since API level 33. On Android 16 devices with apps targeting API level 36 it will no longer be called, so use `OnBackPressedDispatcher` instead. [1]

questions.question: How do I show a native alert with OK and Cancel buttons?
questions.searchedQuestion: How do I show a native alert with OK and Cancel buttons in React Native?

retrieved.headingPath: Alert > Android
Alert > Example
Alert
ActionSheetIOS > Example
BackHandler > Example

questions.answer:
Use `Alert.alert` with a title, a message, and an array of buttons. Each button's `onPress` fires when it's tapped, and tapping any button dismisses the alert [3].

```tsx
import {Alert} from 'react-native';

const createTwoButtonAlert = () =>
  Alert.alert('Alert Title', 'My Alert Msg', [
    {
      text: 'Cancel',
      onPress: () => console.log('Cancel Pressed'),
      style: 'cancel',
    },
    {text: 'OK', onPress: () => console.log('OK Pressed')},
  ]);
```
[2]

**Notes:**
- If you don't pass any buttons, the alert shows a single "OK" button by default [3].
- On Android, with two buttons the first is treated as the 'negative' button and the second as the 'positive' one (such as 'Cancel', 'OK') [1].
- Android alerts can be dismissed by tapping outside the dialog only if you pass `{cancelable: true}` as the options parameter. You can handle that with an `onDismiss` callback in the same options [1].

```tsx
Alert.alert(
  'Alert Title',
  'My Alert Msg',
  [{text: 'Cancel', style: 'cancel'}],
  {
    cancelable: true,
    onDismiss: () => console.log('Dismissed'),
  },
);
```
[1]

`Alert` works on both Android and iOS for static alerts [3].

questions.answer:
If you're using a `ScrollView`, the `horizontal` prop defaults to `false`, so its children are arranged vertically in a column. Set `horizontal={true}` to lay them out in a row [1].

```jsx
<ScrollView horizontal={true}>
```

`FlatList` and `VirtualizedList` work the same way. With `horizontal` set to `true`, items render next to each other instead of stacked vertically [2][3].

```jsx
<FlatList horizontal={true} data={data} renderItem={renderItem} />
```

The docs provided don't explain the default layout of a plain `View` or how to change it, so I can't say why those stack vertically or how to arrange them side by side.

questions.question: How do I generate a signed release build for the Google Play Store?
questions.searchedQuestion: How do I generate a signed release build for the Google Play Store?

retrieved.headingPath: Publishing to Google Play Store > Generating the release AAB

questions.answer:
Run the release build command from your project root:

```shell
npx react-native build-android --mode=release
```

This uses Gradle's `bundleRelease` to bundle all the JavaScript your app needs into an AAB (Android App Bundle). The AAB ends up at `android/app/build/outputs/bundle/release/app-release.aab`, ready to upload to Google Play. [1]

**Things to watch for:**

- Make sure `gradle.properties` doesn't contain `org.gradle.configureondemand=true`, because it makes the release build skip bundling JS and assets. [1]
- If you changed default file/folder names or the project structure, check `android/app/build.gradle` to adjust how the JS bundle and drawable resources are bundled. [1]
- Google Play only accepts the AAB format if App Signing by Google Play is configured in the Google Play Console. [1]
- Before upload, your binary must be signed with an upload key. Google Play can then manage the release signing for you. [5]

**Migrating an existing app:** if your app doesn't use App Signing by Google Play yet, generate a new upload key and update the release signing config in `android/app/build.gradle` to use it. Then follow Google's instructions to send your original release key to Google Play. [2]

**Testing before upload:** uninstall any previous version of the app, then run one of these from the project root: [3]

```shell
npm run android -- --mode="release"
```

```shell
yarn android --mode release
```

`--mode release` only works if you've set up signing. [3]

**Not covered:** the excerpts reference generating an upload key and adding the signing config to Gradle, but they don't include the actual steps or commands for those. [2][5]

questions.question: How do I make a value that's derived from other signals?
questions.searchedQuestion: How do I make a value that's derived from other signals?

retrieved.headingPath: Signal write in a disallowed context > Writing to signals is not allowed in a computed
Form models > Reading model values
Debug the signal graph > Read the graph
Angular Signals > What are signals? > Computed signals
Angular Signals > What are signals? > Computed signals

questions.answer:
Use `computed`. It creates a read-only signal that derives its value from other signals:

```typescript
const count: WritableSignal<number> = signal(0);
const doubleCount: Signal<number> = computed(() => count() * 2);
```

Angular knows `doubleCount` depends on `count`, so it updates whenever `count` changes. [5]

Some behaviors to know:

- **Lazy and memoized:** The derivation doesn't run until the first time you read the computed signal. The result is cached and reused until a dependency changes, so expensive derivations like filtering arrays are safe. [5]
- **Read-only:** You can't call `.set()` on a computed signal. Doing so produces a compilation error. [5]
- **Dynamic dependencies:** Only signals actually read during the derivation are tracked. Dependencies can be added or removed as the derivation runs. [4][5]
- **No side effects:** Don't write to other signals inside a `computed`. Instead of storing a derived value in a separate writable signal, make it a `computed`: [1]

```typescript
count = signal(1);
total = computed(() => this.count() * 2);
```

If the derived value also needs to be writable, use `linkedSignal`. If the write is a side effect of a change, use an `effect`. [1]

questions.answer:
The answer depends on your framework.

**Angular:** Use the built-in `@defer` feature to delay loading a heavy component. It extracts the code of components, directives, and pipes inside the `@defer` block into separate JavaScript chunks. These chunks load only when necessary, based on the triggers you configure [1]. The provided docs don't list which triggers exist, so I can't confirm from them that there is a "scrolls into view" trigger.

**React Native:** `FlatList` renders items lazily, when they are about to appear, and removes items that scroll far off screen to save memory and processing time [2]. By contrast, `ScrollView` renders all its child components at once, which can slow rendering and increase memory use for long content [2]. This applies to items in a list. The provided docs don't describe a way to lazy-load a single standalone component on scroll.
